big: Meena wants ₹50 lakh for her daughter's college, twelve years from now. The cost in twelve years is not ₹50 lakh. It is a bigger number, and the mix of funds has to change as the day nears.

lines: I want ₹50 lakh for my daughter's college in 12 years. How much should I save?
First, the price of that college will rise. Then we choose the funds. Watch both change together.

alt: Twelve bars shifting from equity to safer funds as a cost figure rises with inflation
caps: Each year the price rises with inflation, about 6% in this example.
For the first nine years most of the money can sit in equity.
In the last three years it moves into safer funds, so a fall near the end cannot ruin the goal.
The goal is about ₹1 crore by then, not ₹50 lakh.

q: A college costs ₹50 lakh today. With about 6% yearly inflation, roughly what will it cost in 12 years?
why: ₹53 lakh is one year of inflation, not twelve. The price rises every year, and each rise builds on the last.
₹86 lakh adds 6% of ₹50 lakh for twelve years, without letting each year's rise build on the one before.
Each year multiplies by 1.06, and twelve years gives about double. Inflation compounds, just like returns.
₹62 lakh is far below even the simple sum. Twelve years of rising prices cannot add only a quarter.

q: A family needs a car down payment of ₹4 lakh in 18 months. Where does the money belong?
opts: Mostly in equity, to chase the highest return available
In a low-risk fund such as a liquid or short-duration fund
In a sector fund, since a short goal needs a quick gain
In gold, since gold keeps rising whenever shares fall
why: With 18 months to go, a 20% fall leaves no time to recover, and the car cannot wait for the market.
A short goal needs the money to be steady and easy to get. Low-risk funds fit that need.
Sector funds swing a lot and can stay down for years. That is the opposite of what a short goal needs.
Gold can fall too. No asset only rises, so none is safe to bet a short goal on.

q: Why does the plan move money from equity to safer funds in the last three years before the goal?
opts: Equity stops earning anything in the last three years before a goal
A late fall leaves no time to recover, so what is saved needs protecting
SEBI requires goal-based investments to turn safer as the date nears
Safer funds always earn more than equity near the end of a goal
why: Equity does not stop. The reason is the risk of a fall at the wrong time, not the end of returns.
The closer the date, the less time to recover. Moving to safer funds locks in much of what has been built.
SEBI has no such rule for an ordinary investor's goal. This is a planning habit, not a regulation.
Safer funds usually earn less. The trade is a lower return for a lower risk of loss when it matters.

q: Why keep a separate fund or folio for each goal?
opts: Funds held in separate folios earn higher returns than a single folio
Progress on each goal is easy to see, and no goal is raided for another
It lowers the expense ratio that is charged on each separate folio
It lets the investor skip the yearly review of each goal's plan
why: A folio is only a record. The return depends on the fund, not on how many folios hold it.
With one pot, it is hard to tell which goal is on track and easy to borrow from the wrong one.
Expense ratios are set by the fund and do not change with the number of folios.
Goals change, so each folio still needs a yearly look at income, cost and date.

pts: Write the goal, the amount in future rupees, and the date. Inflate the amount.
Long horizon: more equity. Short horizon: safer funds.
Move to safer funds as the date nears, and review each year.
